name: Test UI
blurb: Browse and iterate the project's proven-component kit — preview variants, read the API, and generate new ones.
prompt:
The Component Library pane is open for this project. It shows the proven-component kit(s) the app is built from — for each component: a live preview, its variants, props/API, what it composes (and is composed by), and its source. Use this stage to review which components the planned features need, spot the gaps still to design, and generate new variants where the kit falls short. This is an app-driven surface: help the user reason about the UI kit and keep it consistent, but do NOT write component code here — the fleet builds against the kit later.

**Pick each feature's layout by its data's SHAPE.** For every data-bearing view, first derive the shape of the data it renders. When the project has a Data Model, DERIVE IT MECHANICALLY instead of judging by eye: `bsc data shapes` (optionally an entity key; `--pretty` for indented JSON) infers each entity's shape from the model's own structure and returns RANKED candidates — each with a confidence (`strong`/`likely`/`possible`) and the reason it fired. Lead with the top candidate; when two are equally plausible (a lone self-referencing ref is a `tree` only if an item has ONE parent, a `graph` otherwise) ask the user — the schema cannot settle it, and a confidently wrong shape is worse than an open question. Without a Data Model, judge the shape from the feature spec. Either way it is one of the seven: `list` (flat ordered collection), `linked-list` (items chained by next/prev), `tree` (single-parent hierarchy), `graph` (nodes + arbitrary edges), `table` (fixed aligned columns), `key-value` (one record's named fields), `series` (an ordered label axis + one or more aligned numeric value series — a time-series). Then query the kit mechanically: `bsc ui shapes <shape>` prints that shape's ideal components (and `bsc ui shapes` the whole vocabulary with coverage); `bsc ui list --shape <shape>` filters the component list to the same set. A shape with NO components is a genuine kit gap — record it as a component to design, do not force a near-fit rendering onto the wrong shape.

**Bake the kit's lint enforcement into the app** so the rules auto-fire during the build. Run `bsc ui eslint-preset --kit <kitId>` to emit the kit's eslint config (`no-restricted-syntax`/`no-restricted-imports` derived from each component — e.g. "use <Button> not a raw <button>"), and author the app's eslint config to EXTEND that preset (write it as a shared preset the app's `eslint.config.*` references). Then ensure the app's CI workflow AND each worker's gate run `lint`, so an agent that hand-rolls a component the kit already provides is auto-flagged and pointed at the kit component. Every rule carries an escape hatch for a justified exception.

**Pair the app with a THEME (#2489).** The kit's look is themeable: run `bsc ui theme list` to enumerate the available themes (`bsc ui theme get <id>` prints one theme's semantic-token overrides). Present the options and choose one WITH the user, then record the app's {kit, theme} pair durably: pipe `{"kit": {"id": "<kit id>", "version": "<kit version>"}, "themeId": "<theme id>"}` into `bsc plan ui set` (the kit halves come from the blueprint's pinned id@version; `themeId` defaults to `default`). The generated app receives its palette FROM that record as two files — `bsc ui emit-css --theme <id> --out <styles dir>` writes `tokens.css` (the semantic token contract layer the kit components consume — read-only for build agents) and `theme.css` (the chosen theme's overrides — THE app's palette). Stylesheet order is the contract: tokens.css → theme.css → app styles, so two apps from the same blueprint differ by exactly theme.css and re-theming an app is swapping that one file (re-run emit-css with another --theme) — zero component changes. The theme resolves BY ID at emission time (`bsc ui theme get` semantics), never snapshotted, so a designer-refined theme applies on the next emit.
directive: **Test UI** — the app builds on a proven-component kit. Review which components the planned features need and spot the gaps to design. For each data-bearing view, derive the data's shape (`list` · `linked-list` · `tree` · `graph` · `table` · `key-value` · `series`) — with a Data Model, `bsc data shapes` infers it from the schema and returns ranked candidates with a confidence + reason (ask the user when the top two tie) — then pick the ideal layout mechanically: `bsc ui shapes <shape>` prints the shape's ideal components, `bsc ui list --shape <shape>` filters the library to them; an uncovered shape is a kit gap to record, not a fit to force. Then BAKE the kit's lint enforcement into the generated app: run `bsc ui eslint-preset --kit <kit>` to emit the kit's eslint config, author the app's eslint config to EXTEND it, and ensure the app's CI + each worker's gate run `lint` — so an agent can't quietly re-invent a component the kit already provides (each rule keeps an escape hatch). Pair the app with a THEME (#2489): `bsc ui theme list`, choose one with the user, then record the {kit, theme} pair via `bsc plan ui set` (JSON on stdin: `{"kit": {"id": "…", "version": "…"}, "themeId": "…"}`). The generated app's palette is emitted from that record — `bsc ui emit-css --theme <id>` produces `tokens.css` (the semantic contract layer, read-only for workers) + `theme.css` (the theme's overrides; stylesheet order tokens.css → theme.css → app styles) — so re-theming an app = swapping theme.css only. Do not write component code in this stage.
